opts: A: Loss of randomisation
B: Premature convergence on a locally good arm, with no ability to detect non-stationarity if conditions change
C: Violation of SUTVA
D: Excessive compute cost
data.explanation: Static bandits assume stationary rewards. Discounted or sliding-window variants retain exploration when the environment shifts.

data.q: What does equalised odds require?
opts: A: Equal accuracy across groups
B: Equal positive prediction rates across groups
C: Equal representation in training data
D: Equal true positive and false positive rates across protected groups
data.explanation: Equalised odds constrains error rates conditional on the true outcome. Demographic parity constrains outcome rates regardless of ground truth.

data.q: What guarantee does differential privacy provide?
opts: A: Data cannot be accessed without authorisation
B: Encryption of data at rest
C: Bounded change in output distribution whether or not any single individual is in the dataset
D: Complete anonymity of all records
data.explanation: The epsilon parameter bounds the privacy loss. It is a mathematical guarantee about inference from outputs, not an access control.

data.q: What is the purpose of a model card?
opts: A: To document code architecture
B: To store model weights
C: To communicate intended use, performance across relevant subgroups, limitations, and ethical considerations
D: To track deployment status
data.explanation: Model cards make scope and failure modes legible to people who did not build the model, which is central to responsible deployment.

data.q: Which element is most often missing from model documentation and most consequential?
opts: A: Explicit statements of out-of-scope use and known failure conditions
B: The training framework version
C: The name of the data scientist
D: The model's parameter count
data.explanation: Misuse outside intended scope is a leading source of real-world harm. Stating what the model must not be used for is the single highest-value section.

data.q: How does the EU AI Act primarily classify obligations?
opts: A: By the developer's country of origin
B: By the training compute used
C: By model size in parameters
D: By risk tier of the use case: unacceptable, high, limited, and minimal risk
data.explanation: Obligations follow the application's risk, not the technology. Separate provisions apply to general-purpose AI models above a compute threshold.

data.q: Your firm deploys AI for CV screening in the EU. What is the likely classification?
opts: A: Outside the Act's scope
B: Prohibited outright
C: High risk, requiring risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight, and conformity assessment
D: Minimal risk
data.explanation: Employment and worker management is explicitly listed as high risk in Annex III, triggering the full compliance regime.

data.q: What is the core principle of three-lines-of-defence model risk management?
opts: A: Models must be retrained quarterly
B: All models are validated by their developers
C: Every model requires board approval
D: Separation of ownership, independent validation, and internal audit into distinct accountable functions
data.explanation: Independence of the validation function from the development team is the structural control that makes the framework meaningful.

data.q: Why can calibration and equalised odds not generally hold simultaneously?
opts: A: Equalised odds requires balanced data
B: They measure the same thing
C: When base rates differ between groups, satisfying one mathematically precludes the other except in degenerate cases
D: Calibration is not a fairness metric
data.explanation: This is the impossibility result from Kleinberg and Chouldechova. The choice between them is a value judgement, not a technical optimisation.

data.q: Your model shows disparate outcomes traced to historically biased training labels. What is the right response?
opts: A: Address the label generation process, and if that is not possible, document the limitation and apply a justified mitigation with monitoring
B: Adjust the decision threshold per group only
C: Remove the protected attribute
D: Accept it as reflecting reality
data.explanation: Bias in the label is upstream of the model. Threshold adjustment may itself raise legal issues, so the choice needs documentation and legal review.

data.q: What is the strongest limitation of pre-processing fairness interventions?
opts: A: They only work on tabular data
B: They cannot guarantee fairness of the final model, since the learning algorithm may reintroduce disparity
C: They require protected attributes
D: They are computationally expensive
data.explanation: Reweighting or resampling shapes inputs, but outcome fairness must still be measured on the trained model's actual predictions.

data.q: What is the fundamental trade-off in differential privacy?
opts: A: Model size versus privacy
B: Privacy budget versus utility: smaller epsilon means stronger privacy and more noise, degrading accuracy
C: Encryption strength versus latency
D: Speed versus storage
data.explanation: Each query consumes budget. Tight budgets protect individuals but can make results too noisy to use, especially on small subgroups.

data.q: When is federated learning the appropriate architecture?
opts: A: Whenever data is large
B: When labels are scarce
C: When you need faster training
D: When raw data cannot leave its source for legal or contractual reasons but a shared model is needed
data.explanation: Federated training moves the model to the data. Note that gradients can still leak information, so secure aggregation or DP is usually layered on.

data.q: Why is k-anonymity insufficient for modern re-identification risk?
opts: A: Homogeneity and background-knowledge attacks can re-identify individuals despite the guarantee, especially with high-dimensional data
B: It only applies to text data
C: It is too computationally expensive
D: It requires removing all attributes
data.explanation: l-diversity and t-closeness patch specific weaknesses, but high-dimensional data remains vulnerable. Differential privacy offers a stronger formal footing.

data.q: What does a datasheet for a dataset document that a model card does not?
opts: A: Model accuracy metrics
B: Collection motivation, composition, consent and labelling process, and known distribution limitations of the data itself
C: Hyperparameters
D: Serving latency
data.explanation: Datasheets travel with the data and let downstream users judge whether it fits their context, independently of any one model.

data.q: What does the NIST AI Risk Management Framework organise its guidance around?
opts: A: Four functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage
B: A required technical standard
C: Three risk tiers
D: A certification scheme
data.explanation: The NIST AI RMF is voluntary and outcome-oriented rather than prescriptive, which is why it is often paired with ISO/IEC 42001 for a certifiable management system.

data.q: Your model is compliant with GDPR. Does that mean it satisfies the EU AI Act?
opts: A: Yes, they cover the same ground
B: No: GDPR governs personal data processing, while the AI Act imposes separate product-safety style obligations on AI systems
C: Only for high-risk systems
D: Yes, if consent was obtained
data.explanation: The two regimes overlap but are distinct. An AI system can be lawful under GDPR and still fail AI Act conformity requirements.

data.q: Which model would be assigned the highest risk tier in a typical MRM framework?
opts: A: A model driving automated credit decisions with direct customer impact and regulatory exposure
B: A model summarising internal documents
C: An internal tool ranking meeting-room bookings
D: A prototype in a research notebook
data.explanation: Tiering considers materiality, customer impact, autonomy of the decision, and regulatory scrutiny, which the credit model maximises on every axis.

data.q: Why must a model inventory include shadow and third-party models?
opts: A: To track licensing costs only
B: To improve model accuracy
C: To simplify procurement
D: Ungoverned models carry the same risk as internal ones, and regulators hold the deploying firm accountable regardless of who built it
data.explanation: Accountability does not transfer with the build. Vendor models need the same validation, monitoring, and documentation as internal ones.

data.q: Design a bias audit cadence for a high-risk production model. What structure is defensible?
opts: A: One audit at launch
B: Annual review by the development team
C: Pre-deployment audit, continuous subgroup performance monitoring, and periodic independent review with documented remediation tracking
D: Audit only after a complaint
data.explanation: Disparity can emerge post-deployment through drift. Continuous measurement plus independent periodic review is what regulators increasingly expect.

data.q: A vendor refuses to disclose training data provenance for a model you plan to deploy in a high-risk use case. How should you treat this?
opts: A: Treat it as a material compliance gap, since you carry the deployer obligations and cannot evidence data governance
B: Accept it as standard commercial confidentiality
C: Escalate only if a problem occurs
D: Deploy with a disclaimer
data.explanation: Deployer obligations cannot be discharged without evidence. Contractual disclosure rights or audit provisions should be secured before deployment.

nontech.q: What is machine learning?
opts: A: Any software that automates a manual task
B: A faster type of database
C: A robot that performs physical work
D: A method where systems learn patterns from data rather than following explicitly written rules
nontech.explanation: The defining feature is learning from examples. Traditional software follows rules a person wrote; machine learning derives its behaviour from data.

nontech.q: Which of these is a machine learning application rather than conventional automation?
opts: A: A spreadsheet formula that sums a column
B: An email filter that learns which messages you treat as spam
C: A form that rejects blank fields
D: A scheduled report that runs every Monday
nontech.explanation: The spam filter improves from your behaviour. The others execute fixed instructions and never change without a person editing them.

nontech.q: How do AI, machine learning, and deep learning relate?
opts: A: They are three names for the same thing
B: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of artificial intelligence
C: AI is a subset of deep learning
D: They are unrelated fields
nontech.explanation: AI is the broad goal, machine learning is one approach to it, and deep learning is a specific family of machine learning using layered neural networks.

nontech.q: What is a large language model?
opts: A: A database of every website
B: A model trained on vast text that predicts likely continuations, producing fluent language
C: A search engine with a chat interface
D: A translation dictionary
nontech.explanation: It generates text by predicting what comes next. It is not looking answers up in a stored table, which is why it can produce plausible but wrong output.

nontech.q: What separates generative AI from predictive AI?
opts: A: Generative AI produces new content; predictive AI estimates an outcome or category from existing data
B: Predictive AI only works with numbers
C: Generative AI is newer
D: They serve identical purposes
nontech.explanation: A churn model outputs a probability; a writing assistant outputs a document. Both are AI but answer different kinds of question.

nontech.q: Which task calls for predictive rather than generative AI?
opts: A: Summarising a long report
B: Drafting a customer apology email
C: Estimating which accounts are likely to cancel next quarter
D: Generating product description variants
nontech.explanation: Estimating a future outcome from historical patterns is prediction. The other three produce new text.

nontech.q: Why does an AI assistant sometimes not know about recent events?
opts: A: Recent events are legally restricted
B: It only stores popular topics
C: Its knowledge comes from data collected up to a cutoff date, unless it can search for current information
D: It is deliberately withholding information
nontech.explanation: Training data has an end date. Tools that search the web at query time are how systems bridge the gap.

nontech.q: Why should you not rely on an AI assistant for precise arithmetic on a long list of figures?
opts: A: It rounds all figures automatically
B: Language models predict text rather than calculate, so they can produce confident but wrong numbers unless a calculator tool is used
C: Numbers are not in its training data
D: It refuses numerical questions
nontech.explanation: Give it the calculation tool, or do the arithmetic in a spreadsheet and ask the model to interpret the result.

nontech.q: What is a hallucination in AI output?
opts: A: A visual error in the interface
B: A refusal to answer
C: Fluent, confident content that is factually wrong or entirely invented
D: A slow response
nontech.explanation: The model optimises for plausible-sounding text, and a fabricated citation looks as convincing as a real one. Verification is the only reliable defence.

nontech.q: In plain terms, how does a model learn during training?
opts: A: It repeatedly adjusts internal settings to reduce the difference between its outputs and the correct answers
B: A person writes rules for every case
C: It memorises the training data exactly
D: It copies another model's behaviour
nontech.explanation: Training is iterative error reduction across millions of examples. This is also why gaps or biases in the data show up in the model.

nontech.q: What is training data?
opts: A: The examples used to teach the model patterns before it is deployed
B: The hardware the model runs on
C: The instructions typed by the user each session
D: The output the model produces
nontech.explanation: Training data shapes what the model can do and what biases it carries. What you type at use time is a prompt, not training data.

nontech.q: Your team wants AI to both forecast demand and write the accompanying commentary. What is the sensible architecture?
opts: A: Neither task suits AI
B: A generative model for the forecast only
C: One generative model doing both
D: A predictive model for the forecast, with a generative model narrating its output
nontech.explanation: Asking a language model to produce numeric forecasts invites fabricated figures. Let the statistical model produce numbers and the language model explain them.

nontech.q: Which task is a poor fit for a general AI assistant without additional safeguards?
opts: A: Making a final decision on an employee's dismissal
B: Brainstorming meeting agenda items
C: Suggesting alternative subject lines
D: Rewriting a paragraph more concisely
nontech.explanation: Consequential decisions about people require human accountability, documented reasoning, and often legal review. AI can support the analysis but not own the decision.

nontech.q: An AI tool gives a different answer to the same question asked twice. Why?
opts: A: Generation involves sampling, so outputs vary unless settings force deterministic behaviour
B: The tool is broken
C: The question was ambiguous both times
D: It learned between the two attempts
nontech.explanation: Variability is a design property, not a defect. It also means output should be verified rather than assumed reproducible.

nontech.q: An AI assistant cites a study with authors, journal, and year. What should you do before using it?
opts: A: Search for the citation independently to confirm the source exists and says what was claimed
B: Use it but add a disclaimer
C: Trust it; that level of detail indicates accuracy
D: Ask the AI whether it is sure
nontech.explanation: Fabricated citations are typically highly specific and well-formatted. Asking the model to self-confirm is unreliable.

nontech.q: Which situation carries the highest hallucination risk?
opts: A: Rephrasing text you supplied
B: Generating brainstorm ideas
C: Asking for specific statistics about a niche topic with no source provided
D: Summarising a document you uploaded
nontech.explanation: Risk rises when the model must supply facts from memory. Grounding it in a document you provide reduces it substantially.

nontech.q: Which prompt change most reduces fabrication risk?
opts: A: Providing the source material and instructing it to answer only from that material and say so if the answer is absent
B: Asking the same question repeatedly
C: Asking the model to be accurate
D: Increasing response length
nontech.explanation: Grounding plus an explicit permission to say I don't know removes the pressure to produce an answer regardless.

nontech.q: Does typing into a company-approved AI assistant retrain the model on your input?
opts: A: Always, immediately
B: Never, under any circumstances
C: It depends on the product and contract terms; enterprise agreements typically exclude customer data from training
D: Only if you tick a box
nontech.explanation: This is a contractual and configuration question, not a technical universal. Check your organisation's terms before entering sensitive material.

nontech.q: A vendor claims their product uses AI to automatically route support tickets. What should you ask first?
opts: A: Where the servers are hosted
B: How many parameters the model has
C: Which programming language it uses
D: What data it was trained on, how accuracy is measured, and what happens when it routes incorrectly
nontech.explanation: Evidence of performance and failure handling matters more than technical internals for a buying decision.

nontech.q: Which statement about AI capability is most accurate?
opts: A: AI reliability improves the longer you use it in a session
B: AI is only useful for simple tasks
C: Performance varies sharply by task, and confident output is not evidence of correctness
D: AI now outperforms humans at nearly all knowledge work
nontech.explanation: Capability is uneven and task-specific. Fluency is a property of the output format, not a signal of accuracy.

nontech.q: What is a prompt?
opts: A: The AI's response
B: The training dataset
C: The instruction or question you give the AI
D: The software licence
nontech.explanation: The prompt is your input. Its clarity and completeness largely determine output quality.

nontech.q: Which prompt will produce the most useful result?
opts: A: Product description please
B: Make it good
C: Write about our product
D: Write a 150-word product description for our project management tool, aimed at small business owners, emphasising ease of setup
nontech.explanation: Length, audience, subject, and emphasis are all specified, so the model does not have to guess.

nontech.q: Why does specifying an audience improve output?
opts: A: It constrains vocabulary, assumed knowledge, and tone to something appropriate
B: It reduces processing cost
C: It is required by most tools
D: It makes the response shorter
nontech.explanation: The same content pitched at a board member and a new graduate should read very differently. Naming the reader resolves that.

nontech.q: Your first output is too formal. What is the most efficient next step?
opts: A: Accept it and edit manually
B: Start a new conversation with a different prompt
C: Try a different AI tool
D: Reply asking for a warmer, more conversational tone, keeping the same structure
nontech.explanation: Iterating within the conversation preserves context. Restarting discards the work already done.

nontech.q: What is the most important habit when reviewing AI output?
opts: A: Checking the word count
B: Verifying factual claims and figures against a trusted source
C: Checking the response arrived quickly
D: Confirming the tone is friendly
nontech.explanation: Fluency is not accuracy. Specific claims, numbers, names, and citations are where errors concentrate.

nontech.q: You need output in a specific layout every time. What should you include?
opts: A: A request to be consistent
B: A higher word count
C: An explicit template or an example of the exact format you want
D: A longer prompt
nontech.explanation: Showing the format is far more reliable than describing it. One worked example resolves most ambiguity.

nontech.q: What does assigning a role in a prompt achieve?
opts: A: It makes the AI genuinely expert
B: It speeds up the response
C: It guarantees factual accuracy
D: It shifts vocabulary, framing, and emphasis toward that perspective
nontech.explanation: Role framing is a stylistic and perspective lever. It does not add knowledge or reduce error rates, so verification still applies.

nontech.q: Which technique best handles a complex request?
opts: A: Repeat the prompt until it improves
B: One long prompt with every requirement
C: Break it into sequential steps, reviewing each before moving on
D: Ask several tools the same question
nontech.explanation: Decomposition lets you correct course early. A single overloaded prompt tends to drop requirements silently.

nontech.q: What does providing examples in a prompt accomplish?
opts: A: It trains the model permanently
B: It removes the need for instructions
C: It reduces the cost per request
D: It demonstrates the pattern you want, which the model imitates for the current task
nontech.explanation: This is in-context learning. It applies to the current conversation only and does not change the underlying model.

nontech.q: Your AI output keeps including a section you do not want. What is the fix?
opts: A: Shorten the prompt
B: Use a different model
C: Delete it manually each time
D: State the exclusion explicitly, describing what to produce instead of only what to avoid
nontech.explanation: Negative-only instructions are less reliable than positive specification. Saying end with the recommendation works better than don't add a conclusion.

nontech.q: You need to turn 30 interview transcripts into a themed summary. What is the sound workflow?
opts: A: Summarise the first three and generalise
B: Summarise each individually against a fixed structure, then synthesise the summaries in a second pass
C: Paste all 30 into one prompt
D: Ask for themes without providing transcripts
nontech.explanation: Chunking keeps each pass within reliable context limits and makes intermediate output checkable.

nontech.q: What does chaining prompts mean?
opts: A: Connecting two AI tools together
B: Using the output of one step as the input to the next in a deliberate sequence
C: Writing very long prompts
D: Running the same prompt repeatedly
nontech.explanation: Each step is simpler and verifiable, which raises reliability on multi-stage work.

nontech.q: Which output element deserves the closest scrutiny?
opts: A: Use of bullet points
B: Paragraph length
C: Specific figures, dates, names, and quoted sources
D: Introductory framing
nontech.explanation: Verifiable specifics are both the highest risk and the easiest to check.

nontech.q: AI-generated content in your team all sounds the same. Why does this matter?
opts: A: It cannot be edited
B: Homogenised output weakens brand voice and signals low effort to readers
C: It uses more tokens
D: It is slower to produce
nontech.explanation: Default model style is recognisable. Supplying voice guidelines and editing meaningfully preserves distinctiveness.

nontech.q: How should you verify a summary of a document you have not read?
opts: A: Ask the AI if the summary is accurate
B: Compare with a second AI's summary
C: Spot-check key claims against the source sections they came from
D: Assume accuracy if it is well written
nontech.explanation: Self-assessment is unreliable, and two models can share the same misreading. Only the source settles it.

nontech.q: Why does an AI sometimes answer a question you did not ask?
opts: A: The tool is overloaded
B: Ambiguous phrasing lets it infer a different intent than you had
C: It ignores instructions deliberately
D: It has a limited vocabulary
nontech.explanation: Ambiguity gets resolved by the model's best guess. Stating the goal and the intended use removes most of it.

nontech.q: When is it worth building a reusable prompt template?
opts: A: Only for technical tasks
B: For a task performed regularly where consistency across people and outputs matters
C: Never; each prompt should be unique
D: For any one-off question
nontech.explanation: Templates encode what worked and remove per-person variation. For recurring work they pay back quickly.

nontech.q: Which part of a document workflow should stay human?
opts: A: Generating a first draft
B: Suggesting alternative phrasings
C: Checking for typos
D: Final approval and sign-off on customer-facing claims
nontech.explanation: Accountability for published claims cannot be delegated to a tool. Drafting and mechanical checks are reasonable to automate.

nontech.q: Your team's AI-assisted process has become slower than doing the work manually. What is the likely cause?
opts: A: Too few people are using it
B: Prompts are too short
C: AI is being applied to tasks where verification costs more than the time saved
D: The AI tool is defective
nontech.explanation: Where verification is expensive and the task is quick, AI adds overhead. Choosing the right tasks matters more than prompt skill.

nontech.q: Your prompt works well for you but produces poor results for a colleague. What is the most likely reason?
opts: A: They are using it at a busier time
B: Your prompt relies on context established earlier in your conversation that theirs lacks
C: Their account has different settings
D: The model treats users differently
nontech.explanation: Prompts that depend on accumulated conversational context are not portable. Reusable prompts must be self-contained.

nontech.q: A chart's y-axis starts at 90 rather than 0. What is the effect?
opts: A: It makes the chart more accurate
B: It visually exaggerates small differences between values
C: It has no effect on interpretation
D: It compresses the differences
nontech.explanation: Truncated axes are a common way to make marginal change look dramatic. Always check the axis range before reacting to a trend.

nontech.q: Which chart type suits showing composition of a total at one point in time?
opts: A: Time series
B: Stacked bar or a simple bar chart of components
C: Scatter plot
D: Line chart
nontech.explanation: Line charts imply change over time. For parts of a whole at a single moment, bars are clearer than pie charts for comparison.

nontech.q: What makes a metric a leading rather than lagging indicator?
opts: A: It is easier to collect
B: It is measured more frequently
C: It appears first on the dashboard
D: It moves before the outcome it predicts, allowing intervention
nontech.explanation: Trial sign-ups lead revenue; last quarter's revenue lags it. Leading indicators support action, lagging ones confirm results.

nontech.q: Why does data quality matter more for AI than for manual analysis?
opts: A: Manual analysis has no quality requirements
B: AI requires more storage
C: Errors and biases in data are learned and applied automatically at scale, without a human noticing
D: AI cannot read messy files
nontech.explanation: A person spots an implausible figure. A model absorbs it as a pattern and reproduces it consistently.

nontech.q: Your customer records have 30% missing values in the industry field. What should you do first?
opts: A: Ignore the field
B: Investigate why it is missing, since a systematic cause changes how you should handle it
C: Delete all incomplete records
D: Fill the gaps with the most common value
nontech.explanation: Missing-not-at-random data biases any analysis. If one signup route never captured the field, dropping those rows removes a whole segment.

nontech.q: What counts as personal data under most privacy regimes?
opts: A: Any information that can identify a person directly or in combination with other data
B: Only data marked confidential
C: Only financial records
D: Only names and addresses
nontech.explanation: Device identifiers, location traces, and combinations of ordinary attributes can all be identifying. The test is identifiability, not sensitivity.

nontech.q: A colleague wants to paste a customer list into a public AI chatbot for analysis. What should you say?
opts: A: Ask the customers first
B: Go ahead if the analysis is useful
C: Remove names but keep everything else
D: Stop: this likely breaches data protection obligations; use an approved tool with appropriate contractual terms
nontech.explanation: Pseudonymisation is often insufficient given re-identification risk. The tool and contract must be approved for that data class.

nontech.q: Average customer spend rose but median spend fell. What does this indicate?
opts: A: A small number of very high spenders is pulling the average up while typical customers spend less
B: The data is wrong
C: Both measures should always move together
D: The sample was too small
nontech.explanation: The mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is not. A divergence is a signal about distribution shape, not an error.

nontech.q: A dashboard shows 40% growth. What is the essential missing context?
opts: A: The name of the data owner
B: The chart colour scheme
C: The refresh frequency
D: The baseline value and time period, since 40% of a tiny number is not meaningful
nontech.explanation: Percentage change without absolute values can dress up trivial movement as a major result.

nontech.q: What does a correlation coefficient of -0.85 tell you?
opts: A: The relationship is weak
B: A strong inverse linear relationship between the two variables
C: There is no relationship
D: One variable causes the other to fall
nontech.explanation: It describes direction and strength of a linear association only. It says nothing about causation or non-linear relationships.

nontech.q: Which is the better primary metric for a subscription business?
opts: A: Number of features shipped
B: Total registered accounts ever created
C: Website page views
D: Monthly active subscribers and net revenue retention
nontech.explanation: Cumulative counts only ever rise and hide churn. Active usage and retention reflect actual business health.

nontech.q: Your team hits its call-volume target but customer satisfaction falls. What has happened?
opts: A: Call volume is the wrong metric to track at all
B: The satisfaction survey is faulty
C: The metric is being optimised at the expense of the outcome it was meant to represent
D: Both should be ignored
nontech.explanation: This is Goodhart's law. Pairing volume targets with a quality counter-metric prevents the distortion.

nontech.q: What is the purpose of a counter-metric?
opts: A: To simplify reporting
B: To detect harm caused by over-optimising the primary metric
C: To provide a backup if the main metric fails
D: To compare against competitors
nontech.explanation: Speed targets paired with an error-rate counter-metric, for example, keep the optimisation honest.

nontech.q: Which is an example of survivorship bias?
opts: A: Weighting responses by segment size
B: Analysing only customers who are still active to understand retention drivers
C: Using a random sample of all customers
D: Including both won and lost deals
nontech.explanation: The churned customers hold the information you need. Studying only survivors systematically misses the causes of failure.

nontech.q: What is sampling bias?
opts: A: Measuring the wrong variable
B: Taking too small a sample
C: The sample is not representative of the population it is used to draw conclusions about
D: Rounding errors
nontech.explanation: A voluntary online survey overrepresents the engaged and the aggrieved. Size does not fix an unrepresentative sample.

nontech.q: What is data minimisation?
opts: A: Reducing the number of data sources
B: Collecting and retaining only the data necessary for the stated purpose
C: Compressing files to save storage
D: Deleting all data annually
nontech.explanation: It is a core principle in GDPR and similar regimes, and it also reduces breach exposure.

nontech.q: Your team wants to keep conversation logs indefinitely for quality improvement. What is the issue?
opts: A: Indefinite retention conflicts with purpose limitation and retention-period requirements, and increases breach exposure
B: Logs are hard to search
C: There is no issue
D: Storage cost
nontech.explanation: A defined retention period tied to the stated purpose is required under most frameworks and is good practice regardless.

nontech.q: A vendor reports 99% accuracy for their fraud detection model. Why is this insufficient?
opts: A: The figure is probably fabricated
B: 99% is too low for fraud
C: Accuracy is never a valid measure
D: With rare fraud, a model that flags nothing scores near 99% while catching zero cases
nontech.explanation: Ask for detection rate and false positive rate. Accuracy on imbalanced problems is close to meaningless.

nontech.q: Your AI tool performs well in testing and poorly in production. What data issue is most likely?
opts: A: Test data did not reflect real-world input variety, so the model met conditions it never saw
B: Production servers are slower
C: The prompt changed
D: The model is too small
nontech.explanation: Clean, curated test data flatters performance. Real inputs are messier, more varied, and often differently distributed.

nontech.q: Two reports give different figures for the same metric. What is the most productive first step?
opts: A: Compare the definitions, filters, and time windows behind each figure
B: Use the more favourable figure
C: Average the two
D: Escalate to leadership immediately
nontech.explanation: Most discrepancies come from definitional differences, not errors. Agreeing the definition usually resolves it.

nontech.q: Which describes a general-purpose AI assistant?
opts: A: A scheduling application
B: A tool restricted to one task such as translation
C: A conversational tool that handles drafting, summarising, analysis, and question answering across domains
D: A database query interface
nontech.explanation: Breadth across tasks in one conversational interface is the defining characteristic.

nontech.q: Which task suits an AI assistant with document upload?
opts: A: Approving an expense claim
B: Updating a customer record
C: Summarising a 60-page vendor contract and flagging unusual clauses for review
D: Processing a payment
nontech.explanation: It surfaces items for human review. Transactional system actions belong to the systems that own them.

nontech.q: Which document task is AI most reliably good at?
opts: A: Verifying legal compliance of a contract
B: Producing a structured first draft you will review and revise
C: Signing off on financial statements
D: Guaranteeing factual accuracy of statistics
nontech.explanation: Drafting speed is the reliable gain. Assurance and sign-off require accountable human judgement.

nontech.q: What does a no-code automation platform allow?
opts: A: Writing production software without training
B: Replacing all IT systems
C: Training custom AI models
D: Building workflows that connect applications through a visual interface
nontech.explanation: It lowers the barrier for connecting existing tools. It does not remove the need for governance or error handling.

nontech.q: Why is uploading a document usually better than pasting a long excerpt?
opts: A: Pasting is not supported
B: It looks more professional
C: It processes faster
D: The full document preserves structure and surrounding context, reducing misinterpretation
nontech.explanation: Excerpts strip the context that determines meaning, especially in contracts and reports.

nontech.q: Your assistant gives a plausible answer about an internal policy. What should you do?
opts: A: Act on it
B: Check the actual policy document, since the tool has no access to internal policies unless connected
C: Ask it to double-check
D: Share it with the team
nontech.explanation: Without an explicit connection to your systems, any internal detail is inferred rather than retrieved.

nontech.q: You need consistent formatting across 50 generated documents. What is most effective?
opts: A: A fixed template with defined sections supplied in every prompt
B: Using the same tool each time
C: Asking for consistency in each prompt
D: Generating each individually and reformatting after
nontech.explanation: Explicit structure produces far more consistency than a request to be consistent.

nontech.q: AI-generated meeting minutes omitted a decision that was discussed. Why might this happen?
opts: A: Summarisation compresses, and importance is inferred rather than known, so unemphasised items can be dropped
B: The tool is faulty
C: The recording quality was poor
D: Minutes cannot be automated
nontech.explanation: Telling the tool in advance which categories must always be captured, such as decisions and owners, reduces omissions.

nontech.q: You want AI to analyse a spreadsheet of sales figures. What is the safest approach?
opts: A: Use a tool that executes code or formulas on the file, and verify key figures independently
B: Trust the narrative summary
C: Ask it to estimate the trend
D: Ask it to calculate totals from the pasted numbers
nontech.explanation: Computation should be done by something that actually computes. Language-only estimation of figures is unreliable.

nontech.q: What is the main advantage of an AI tool connected to your live data?
opts: A: Answers are grounded in current, actual records rather than inferred from general knowledge
B: It runs faster
C: It is cheaper
D: It requires no prompts
nontech.explanation: Connection turns speculation into retrieval. It also introduces access-control questions that must be handled.

nontech.q: Which process is the best candidate for automation?
opts: A: A task with constantly changing requirements
B: A judgement-heavy decision made twice a year
C: A high-volume, rule-based, repetitive task with clear inputs and outputs
D: A task requiring negotiation
nontech.explanation: Automation pays back on volume and stability. Volatile or judgement-heavy processes cost more to maintain than they save.

nontech.q: What is the main risk of unmanaged AI automation built by individual staff?
opts: A: Shadow processes with no documentation, owner, error handling, or oversight, which fail invisibly when the builder leaves
B: It costs too much
C: It uses too much storage
D: It is too slow
nontech.explanation: Shadow IT concentrates operational risk in undocumented workflows. A lightweight registration and review process addresses it.

nontech.q: Two AI assistants give conflicting answers to a factual question. What do you conclude?
opts: A: Average the two answers
B: The more confident answer is correct
C: The more detailed answer is correct
D: Neither is verified; check an authoritative source
nontech.explanation: Agreement between models is not evidence either, since they can share the same training biases.

nontech.q: Before rolling out an AI analytics tool to non-technical staff, what matters most?
opts: A: The number of features
B: The vendor's market share
C: Interface aesthetics
D: Clear guidance on what the tool can and cannot be trusted with, plus a verification habit
nontech.explanation: Misplaced confidence is the main risk in broad rollouts. Calibrated expectations matter more than features.

nontech.q: Which control should any AI automation touching customer communication have?
opts: A: Human review before send, plus logging and a kill switch
B: A colour-coded dashboard
C: Approval from the builder only
D: A weekly summary email
nontech.explanation: Review, auditability, and the ability to stop it quickly are the minimum for anything customer-facing.

nontech.q: When should AI not be used to draft a communication?
opts: A: Meeting summaries
B: Newsletter copy
C: Sensitive personnel matters where tone, confidentiality, and legal exposure require direct human judgement
D: Routine internal updates
nontech.explanation: Sensitivity and confidentiality outweigh drafting convenience, and such matters often carry legal implications.

nontech.q: An AI tool produces a chart that contradicts your team's known figures. What is the first check?
opts: A: Republish the AI figure
B: Assume the AI found something new
C: Discard the tool
D: Confirm which data source, filters, and date range the tool actually used
nontech.explanation: Most contradictions come from scope differences rather than genuine discovery.

nontech.q: Your automation has run without error for six months. What still needs periodic review?
opts: A: Whether upstream systems, business rules, or data formats have changed in ways it does not detect
B: The naming convention
C: The visual layout
D: Nothing, if it works
nontech.explanation: Silent failure after an upstream change is the common failure mode. No errors is not the same as correct output.

nontech.q: You want an AI assistant to follow your team's writing style consistently. What is most effective?
opts: A: Asking for a professional tone each time
B: Using shorter prompts
C: Supplying a short style guide with two or three example passages in the prompt or saved settings
D: Correcting each output manually
nontech.explanation: Concrete examples convey voice far better than adjectives.

nontech.q: What is the strongest argument for keeping a human in an AI-assisted reporting workflow?
opts: A: It reduces licence costs
B: It is faster
C: Regulations require a signature
D: A human recognises when a plausible-looking result is implausible in context, which the tool cannot
nontech.explanation: Domain context is what catches results that are internally consistent but wrong in reality.

nontech.q: Where does bias in AI systems usually originate?
opts: A: Hardware limitations
B: Random errors
C: Patterns in historical training data that reflect existing inequities, plus design and deployment decisions
D: Deliberate programming choices
nontech.explanation: Models learn the world as recorded. If past decisions were skewed, the model reproduces the skew at scale.

nontech.q: An AI writing tool consistently describes nurses as women and engineers as men. What is this?
opts: A: A prompt formatting problem
B: A random error
C: Correct statistical reporting
D: Representational bias learned from patterns in the training data
nontech.explanation: Reproducing a statistical association as a default assumption is a well-documented harm, distinct from reporting a statistic.

nontech.q: What should an organisational AI use policy cover?
opts: A: Approved tools, permitted data classes, required human review, and disclosure expectations
B: Only the IT department's responsibilities
C: Only technical configuration
D: Only which tools are banned
nontech.explanation: A usable policy tells people what they may do and under what conditions, not just what is prohibited.

nontech.q: You used AI to draft a client-facing analysis. What is your responsibility?
opts: A: Responsibility only for the final paragraph
B: None; the tool produced it
C: Shared responsibility with the vendor
D: Full responsibility for accuracy and appropriateness, as if you had written it yourself
nontech.explanation: Tool use does not transfer accountability. You are answerable for what you send.

nontech.q: What does human-in-the-loop mean?
opts: A: A person reviews or approves AI outputs before they take effect
B: A person monitors system uptime
C: Humans and AI work in separate teams
D: AI assists a person's typing
nontech.explanation: The defining feature is a human decision point in the path between AI output and consequence.

nontech.q: An AI chatbot cannot answer a customer's question. What is the correct design?
opts: A: Provide a best guess
B: End the conversation
C: Acknowledge the limitation and hand off to a human agent with the conversation context
D: Redirect to the FAQ page
nontech.explanation: Graceful escalation with context preserved avoids both fabrication and forcing the customer to repeat themselves.

nontech.q: What is the main IP concern with AI-generated content?
opts: A: It is always plagiarised
B: Ownership and copyrightability vary by jurisdiction, and output may resemble protected material
C: It cannot be used commercially
D: It has no IP implications
nontech.explanation: Several jurisdictions require human authorship for copyright. Substantial similarity to training material is a separate risk.

nontech.q: You notice AI-generated candidate summaries emphasise different qualities by apparent gender. What should you do?
opts: A: Adjust prompts and continue
B: Use it only for shortlisted candidates
C: Manually correct each summary
D: Stop using it for that purpose, document the finding, and escalate to whoever owns AI governance
nontech.explanation: Recruitment is a high-risk use with legal exposure. Ad hoc prompt fixes do not discharge the obligation to investigate.

nontech.q: Why is testing an AI tool only on your own team insufficient?
opts: A: Testing must be automated
B: It takes too long
C: A narrow user group will not surface failures affecting populations unlike them
D: Colleagues are biased reviewers
nontech.explanation: Harms concentrate in groups absent from testing. Representative evaluation is the only way to find them.

nontech.q: When should AI involvement in a work product be disclosed?
opts: A: Only for external documents
B: Never
C: Always, in every document
D: When it is material to the reader's evaluation of the work, or where policy, contract, or regulation requires it
nontech.explanation: Blanket rules fit poorly. Materiality plus applicable obligations is the practical test, and organisational policy should make it concrete.

nontech.q: A colleague submits AI-generated work as entirely their own analysis. What is the core issue?
opts: A: Misrepresentation of provenance, which undermines trust and may breach policy
B: Their choice of tool
C: The time saved
D: The output quality
nontech.explanation: The problem is the false claim about how the work was produced, independent of whether the output is good.

nontech.q: Which decision should never be fully automated without human review?
opts: A: Suggesting related articles
B: Formatting a report
C: Sorting incoming email by topic
D: Denying an individual's insurance claim
nontech.explanation: Decisions with significant individual effect require human involvement, and several jurisdictions grant an explicit right to it.

nontech.q: Why does automation bias make human review less effective over time?
opts: A: Reviewers get faster
B: People increasingly defer to system output and stop scrutinising it, especially when it is usually right
C: The AI becomes more accurate
D: Reviews become mandatory
nontech.explanation: Rubber-stamping is a documented failure mode. Sampling audits and periodic calibration counter it.

nontech.q: Before using AI-generated images in a marketing campaign, what should you confirm?
opts: A: The tool's commercial-use terms, indemnification provisions, and whether the output resembles protected works
B: That they look professional
C: The file resolution
D: The generation date
nontech.explanation: Licence terms and indemnity differ substantially between providers and are the practical control.

nontech.q: Why is pasting a licensed third-party report into an AI tool risky?
opts: A: It may breach the licence terms and expose the content to a third party's retention and processing
B: The tool cannot read PDFs
C: It slows the tool down
D: The formatting is lost
nontech.explanation: Licence terms typically restrict redistribution and processing. Sharing with an external service can constitute both.

nontech.q: A vendor says their model is unbiased because it does not use gender or ethnicity as inputs. Is this adequate?
opts: A: Only for regulated industries
B: No: correlated proxies can reconstruct those attributes, so outcomes must be measured by group
C: Yes, removing the attributes solves it
D: Yes, if documented
nontech.explanation: Fairness is measured in outcomes, not inputs. Removing the attribute can even make disparity harder to detect.

nontech.q: Your organisation has no AI policy but staff are using AI tools widely. What is the most urgent risk?
opts: A: Reduced productivity
B: Confidential or personal data being entered into unapproved tools with unknown retention and training terms
C: Inconsistent formatting
D: Wasted licence spend
nontech.explanation: Data leaving the organisation under unknown terms is difficult to reverse and carries regulatory consequences.

nontech.q: What makes human oversight meaningful rather than nominal?
opts: A: A high review volume
B: Fast review turnaround
C: Reviewers with the authority, information, time, and competence to actually overturn the output
D: A required sign-off field
nontech.explanation: Without genuine capacity to disagree, oversight is a formality. This is explicitly addressed in the EU AI Act's oversight provisions.

nontech.q: Your team wants to fine-tune a model on customer support transcripts. What must be checked first?
opts: A: Model size
B: Consent basis, contractual permissions, personal data handling, and whether transcripts can lawfully be used for this purpose
C: The number of transcripts
D: The training cost
nontech.explanation: Data collected for service delivery is not automatically usable for model training. Purpose limitation applies.

nontech.q: How can a non-technical team contribute meaningfully to fairness review of an AI tool?
opts: A: By checking the vendor's certifications only
B: By reviewing the source code
C: By testing with realistic cases from underrepresented groups and documenting where output quality differs
D: By requesting the model architecture
nontech.explanation: Domain testing surfaces context-specific harms that technical metrics miss. It requires no code access.

manager.q: What should anchor an AI roadmap?
opts: A: Business problems with measurable value, sequenced by feasibility and data readiness
B: Competitor announcements
C: The most advanced techniques available
D: The vendor's product release schedule
manager.explanation: Technology-led roadmaps produce demos without adoption. Starting from a costed business problem keeps the portfolio accountable.

manager.q: Your organisation has 20 proposed AI use cases and capacity for three. What is the most defensible selection method?
opts: A: Let each business unit choose one
B: Score all 20 on business impact, data readiness, technical feasibility, and time-to-value, then stack-rank with stakeholder input
C: Select the three the CEO mentioned
D: Pick the three with the highest projected revenue
manager.explanation: Multi-criteria scoring exposes the trade-offs and creates a record you can defend when a rejected sponsor challenges the decision.

manager.q: Why does data readiness so often derail AI roadmaps?
opts: A: Value cases are approved on business merit while the cost of making data usable is discovered later
B: Data is expensive to store
C: Regulations block data access
D: Data teams are understaffed
manager.explanation: Data preparation frequently dominates delivery effort. Assessing readiness during prioritisation, not after approval, prevents the surprise.

manager.q: What characterises a hub-and-spoke AI operating model?
opts: A: Each unit works independently
B: All AI is outsourced
C: All AI work is done centrally
D: A central function sets standards, platform, and governance while embedded practitioners deliver within business units
manager.explanation: It balances consistency with domain proximity. Fully centralised models create bottlenecks; fully federated ones duplicate effort and diverge on standards.

manager.q: What is the most common cause of failed AI adoption?
opts: A: Poor model accuracy
B: Workflow and change management failures: the tool does not fit how people actually work
C: Insufficient compute
D: Vendor selection errors
manager.explanation: Technically sound systems routinely go unused. Adoption depends on workflow integration, incentives, and trust more than on model quality.

manager.q: A well-performing AI tool has 12% adoption after three months. What should you investigate first?
opts: A: Whether it fits existing workflows, whether users trust it, and whether incentives reward its use
B: Server capacity
C: Model accuracy metrics
D: The training data
manager.explanation: At 12%, the barrier is behavioural or procedural. Technical investigation will not surface a workflow mismatch.

manager.q: A competitor announces a major AI capability. What is the appropriate first response?
opts: A: Assess whether it addresses a real customer need in your context and whether you have the data and capability to compete meaningfully
B: Announce a similar initiative
C: Match it immediately
D: Ignore it
manager.explanation: Announcements often outrun delivery. Reactive matching allocates budget to someone else's strategy.

manager.q: What does the parsimony principle imply for model selection?
opts: A: Use the smallest available dataset
B: Prefer the simplest model that meets the requirement, since simpler models are easier to explain, maintain, audit, and deploy
C: Always use the cheapest option
D: Avoid machine learning where possible
manager.explanation: Complexity should be earned by demonstrated, validated improvement. Total cost of ownership, not just accuracy, is the decision basis.

manager.q: Your AI portfolio has 15 pilots and no production deployments after 18 months. What does this indicate?
opts: A: Pilot purgatory: no path to production, unclear ownership, or no operational funding beyond the pilot stage
B: The technology is immature
C: Healthy experimentation
D: Insufficient budget
manager.explanation: Sustained pilot volume without deployment is a governance failure, not a technical one. Production criteria and ownership must be defined before a pilot starts.

manager.q: Your fully centralised AI team is a bottleneck and business units are building shadow solutions. What is the appropriate structural response?
opts: A: Move to hub-and-spoke: retain central standards and platform, embed practitioners in units, and formalise the shadow work
B: Enforce the central model more strictly
C: Freeze all new AI work
D: Fully decentralise all AI capability
manager.explanation: Shadow activity signals unmet demand. Suppressing it drives it further underground; channelling it into a governed model captures it.

manager.q: What is the main risk of a fully federated AI model with no central function?
opts: A: Too much innovation
B: Reduced business alignment
C: Slower delivery
D: Divergent standards, duplicated spend, inconsistent risk controls, and no organisation-wide view of model exposure
manager.explanation: Federation optimises local speed at the cost of aggregate control. Regulators expect an enterprise view that federation alone does not provide.

manager.q: Staff fear an AI tool will eliminate their roles. What is the most effective managerial response?
opts: A: Mandate usage with performance consequences
B: Avoid the topic
C: Reassure them no jobs will be lost
D: Be specific and honest about which tasks change, how roles evolve, and what retraining is available, then follow through
manager.explanation: Unbacked reassurance destroys credibility when circumstances change. Specificity plus visible investment in transition is what builds trust.

manager.q: Which metric best indicates genuine AI adoption rather than nominal usage?
opts: A: Number of licences issued
B: Training sessions delivered
C: Total logins
D: Repeat use by the same individuals over time on real work, and measurable effect on the target process
manager.explanation: Licences and logins measure exposure. Sustained repeat use on live work is the signal that the tool earned its place.

manager.q: Where is durable competitive advantage from AI most likely to come from?
opts: A: The size of the AI team
B: Proprietary data, workflow integration, and accumulated deployment learning that competitors cannot buy
C: Being first to announce
D: Access to the largest available model
manager.explanation: Frontier models are broadly available. What differentiates is the data and organisational capability wrapped around them.

manager.q: Your team proposes a deep learning model that beats logistic regression by 0.8% AUC. As the decision maker, what do you weigh?
opts: A: The novelty of the approach
B: The team's enthusiasm
C: Whether 0.8% translates into material business value, against added explainability, maintenance, and regulatory burden
D: Only the accuracy improvement
manager.explanation: In regulated contexts an explainable model with marginally lower accuracy is frequently the better overall choice.

manager.q: When does the added complexity of a sophisticated model clearly justify itself?
opts: A: When competitors use it
B: When the team wants to learn the technique
C: When the performance gain converts to significant measured value and the operational and compliance burden is acceptable
D: When compute budget is available
manager.explanation: The test is value net of lifetime cost, evidenced rather than assumed.

manager.q: How should build-versus-buy be decided for an AI capability?
opts: A: Decide by cost alone
B: Always build for control
C: Always buy for speed
D: Build where the capability is differentiating and you have data advantage; buy where it is commodity infrastructure
manager.explanation: Building commodity capability consumes scarce talent. Buying your differentiator hands the advantage to a vendor serving your competitors too.

manager.q: You must design AI governance for a 5,000-person firm with three regulated business lines. What structure fits?
opts: A: Tiered governance: lightweight review for low-risk internal tools, full validation and independent sign-off for high-risk customer-facing models
B: Delegate entirely to each business line
C: A single central approval committee for all AI work
D: Governance only for customer-facing systems
manager.explanation: Uniform heavy process throttles low-risk work and drives shadow adoption. Risk-proportionate tiering is what makes governance sustainable.

manager.q: Your AI programme delivers measurable efficiency but staff report increased workload. What is likely happening?
opts: A: Verification and exception handling has shifted work rather than removing it, and the saved time is not reflected in role design
B: Training was insufficient
C: Staff are resisting change
D: The measurement is wrong
manager.explanation: Efficiency at task level does not automatically reduce workload. Role redesign has to follow the technology change or the gain is not realised.

manager.q: Design a review cadence keeping AI strategy current in a fast-moving field. What is appropriate?
opts: A: Monthly full strategy rewrite
B: Quarterly portfolio review against outcomes, with a standing capability watch and a defined trigger for out-of-cycle reassessment
C: Review only when a competitor moves
D: Annual strategy refresh only
manager.explanation: Annual cycles are too slow and continuous rewriting prevents delivery. Quarterly review with event triggers balances both.

manager.q: What is the purpose of an AI governance framework?
opts: A: To establish accountable roles, policies, and controls so AI is developed and deployed responsibly and in compliance
B: To slow down AI adoption
C: To automate compliance reporting
D: To centralise technical decisions in IT
manager.explanation: Governance defines who is accountable for what. Well-designed, it accelerates safe deployment by removing case-by-case ambiguity.

manager.q: How is the NIST AI Risk Management Framework structured?
opts: A: As three risk tiers
B: Around four functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage
C: As a technical specification
D: As a certification standard with audit requirements
manager.explanation: It is voluntary and outcome-based, so it adapts across sectors. ISO/IEC 42001 provides the certifiable management-system counterpart.

manager.q: How do ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI RMF differ in practical use?
opts: A: NIST is mandatory in the EU
B: ISO 42001 applies only to model developers
C: They are interchangeable
D: ISO 42001 is a certifiable management system standard; NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance on risk practices
manager.explanation: Organisations commonly use NIST for risk practice and ISO 42001 where third-party certification is commercially or contractually required.

manager.q: Your firm deploys AI for credit scoring in the EU. What classification applies?
opts: A: Minimal risk
B: High risk, requiring risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, and conformity assessment
C: Prohibited
D: Limited risk with transparency obligations only
manager.explanation: Creditworthiness assessment is listed in Annex III, triggering the full high-risk regime for deployers and providers.

manager.q: Which AI practices does the EU AI Act prohibit outright?
opts: A: Practices such as social scoring by public authorities and certain manipulative or exploitative systems
B: All facial recognition
C: Generative AI in customer service
D: Any use of personal data
manager.explanation: The unacceptable-risk tier is a narrow list of prohibited practices, distinct from the much broader high-risk category.

manager.q: What should a bias audit examine?
opts: A: Only user complaints
B: Outcome disparities across relevant groups at the decision point, with documented methodology and thresholds
C: Only the training data composition
D: Only the model architecture
manager.explanation: Data review is a necessary input, but the harm materialises in decisions, so outcomes are what must be measured.

manager.q: Why must a model inventory include vendor and embedded AI?
opts: A: Regulatory accountability sits with the deploying organisation regardless of who built the system
B: For licence cost tracking
C: To standardise on one vendor
D: To negotiate better contracts
manager.explanation: Unregistered vendor AI is a common gap. It carries the same obligations as internally built systems.

manager.q: What minimum documentation should exist for every production model?
opts: A: A performance dashboard
B: Purpose and scope, owner, data sources, validation evidence, known limitations, monitoring plan, and review date
C: The source code
D: The vendor contract
manager.explanation: This set answers the questions an auditor, regulator, or successor owner will ask.

manager.q: What is prompt injection?
opts: A: A model training technique
B: Adversarial instructions embedded in content the model processes, causing it to act against the operator's intent
C: A method of improving prompt quality
D: A form of SQL injection
manager.explanation: Indirect injection through retrieved documents, emails, or web pages is particularly dangerous for tool-using agents.

manager.q: Your board asks for assurance that AI risk is under control. What evidence is most credible?
opts: A: A statement that policies exist
B: A current model inventory with risk tiers, evidence of validation and monitoring, incident history, and open remediation items
C: The size of the AI team
D: A vendor certification
manager.explanation: Assurance requires evidence of operating controls, not documented intent.

manager.q: You purchase a high-risk AI system from a vendor. What obligations remain yours?
opts: A: Only if you modify the system
B: Only contractual obligations
C: Deployer obligations including human oversight, input data relevance, monitoring, logging, and worker notification
D: None; the provider bears them
manager.explanation: The Act splits provider and deployer duties. Procurement does not transfer deployer responsibility.

manager.q: Your GDPR compliance programme is mature. What does that cover for AI Act purposes?
opts: A: Nothing relevant
B: Personal data processing only; the AI Act adds separate product-safety style obligations that GDPR does not address
C: All high-risk requirements
D: Everything required
manager.explanation: They overlap on data governance but are distinct regimes with different triggers and different obligations.

manager.q: Your claims model shows different approval rates across demographic groups. What is your first obligation?
opts: A: Adjust thresholds per group immediately
B: Initiate a documented bias investigation, assess legal exposure, and pause expansion pending findings
C: Accept it if overall accuracy is high
D: Remove demographic data from the model
manager.explanation: Per-group threshold adjustment can itself create legal exposure. Investigation, legal input, and documentation come first.

manager.q: Why should bias audits recur rather than happen once at launch?
opts: A: Initial audits are unreliable
B: Population drift, changing usage, and retraining can introduce disparity that did not exist at launch
C: Auditors require repeat business
D: Regulations mandate quarterly audits universally
manager.explanation: A model's fairness properties are not fixed. Continuous subgroup monitoring plus periodic independent review is the defensible pattern.

manager.q: A regulator requests the basis for an automated decision made 14 months ago. What must you produce?
opts: A: A general policy statement
B: The current model version
C: The vendor's documentation
D: The model version in force at that time, the input data, the decision logic, and evidence of oversight
manager.explanation: Point-in-time reconstruction requires retention of versioned artefacts and inference records, which must be designed in advance.

manager.q: Your AI agent can read email and access internal systems. What control matters most?
opts: A: A stricter system prompt
B: A larger model
C: Least-privilege tool permissions and human approval for consequential actions, treating all retrieved content as untrusted
D: Longer output logs
manager.explanation: Prompt-level instructions are advisory. Permission boundaries are enforceable and limit the damage a successful injection can cause.

manager.q: What risk does an employee pasting confidential material into a consumer AI tool create?
opts: A: Loss of control over confidential data under unknown retention and processing terms, potentially breaching contracts and privacy law
B: Reduced output quality
C: Increased licence cost
D: Slower response times
manager.explanation: This is one of the most common real AI incidents. Approved tooling with enterprise terms is the practical control.

manager.q: What is model extraction and why should it concern you?
opts: A: Copying model files from a server
B: Systematically querying a deployed model to reconstruct its behaviour, eroding proprietary advantage
C: Removing a model from production
D: Extracting features from data
manager.explanation: API rate limiting, output perturbation, and anomaly detection on query patterns are the usual mitigations.

manager.q: Design a risk tiering scheme for AI systems in your firm. Which dimensions matter most?
opts: A: Development effort and team size
B: Impact on individuals, decision autonomy, reversibility, regulatory exposure, and scale of use
C: Vendor reputation
D: Model size and training cost
manager.explanation: Tiering should track potential harm, not technical characteristics. A simple model making autonomous consequential decisions outranks a complex advisory one.

manager.q: An internal audit finds your AI governance policy is comprehensive but rarely followed. What is the real problem?
opts: A: Controls are not embedded in delivery workflows, and there is no accountable owner or consequence for bypass
B: The audit was too strict
C: Staff need more training
D: The policy needs rewriting in more detail
manager.explanation: Policy adherence depends on making the compliant path the easy path, with clear ownership. More documentation does not fix that.

manager.q: You are building an AI capability from zero. What is the strongest first hire sequence?
opts: A: A large offshore team
B: Only PhD researchers
C: A data engineer and an ML engineer to establish data foundations and delivery, then specialists as use cases mature
D: Five ML engineers immediately
manager.explanation: Most early AI failures are data infrastructure failures. Research specialists hired before foundations exist are underutilised.

manager.q: What distinguishes an ML engineer from a data scientist in practice?
opts: A: ML engineers focus on productionising, scaling, and operating models; data scientists focus on analysis and model development
B: They are identical roles
C: ML engineers have more education
D: Data scientists write no code
manager.explanation: The boundary varies by organisation, but the production-versus-exploration distinction is the useful one for team design.

manager.q: Why does standard Scrum fit ML work imperfectly?
opts: A: Scrum forbids experimentation
B: Research and experimentation outcomes are not reliably estimable in advance, so fixed-scope sprints break down
C: ML teams work faster
D: ML requires no planning
manager.explanation: Time-boxed exploration with explicit decision gates works better than committing to uncertain outcomes as sprint deliverables.

manager.q: What is technical debt in an ML system?
opts: A: The cost of cloud compute
B: Accumulated shortcuts such as undocumented pipelines, hardcoded features, and untested code that slow future work and raise failure risk
C: The cost of hiring engineers
D: Licence fees for tooling
manager.explanation: ML adds distinctive forms of debt: entanglement between features, undeclared consumers of model output, and pipeline sprawl.

manager.q: An AI project stalls because the data science and engineering teams disagree on deployment approach. What is the managerial fix?
opts: A: Let the more senior team decide
B: Escalate to the CTO
C: Establish a shared definition of done for production readiness, with joint ownership of the deployment path
D: Separate the teams further
manager.explanation: Disagreement usually reflects different implicit standards. Making the standard explicit and shared resolves it structurally.

manager.q: Why is domain expertise essential on an AI team?
opts: A: To provide business context for meetings
B: Domain experts identify when a technically valid result is implausible, and define what the model should actually optimise
C: To approve budgets
D: To handle stakeholder relationships
manager.explanation: Most costly modelling errors are framing errors invisible to technical review but obvious to a practitioner.

manager.q: How should you develop a strong analyst into an ML practitioner?
opts: A: Give them a research project alone
B: Send them on a course and reassign them
C: Promote them and see what happens
D: Structured pairing on real production work with a defined progression path and explicit review points
manager.explanation: Applied capability develops through supervised delivery. Courses build vocabulary, not judgement.

manager.q: Your AI hiring pipeline yields strong researchers but delivery stalls. What capability is missing?
opts: A: More budget
B: More researchers
C: Engineering capability for deployment, monitoring, and integration, plus product ownership translating problems into scoped work
D: Better management
manager.explanation: Research talent without delivery capability produces notebooks. The gap is engineering and product, not research depth.

manager.q: How should you assess an AI engineering candidate beyond technical skill?
opts: A: Evidence of shipping and operating systems in production, and judgement about when not to use ML
B: Years of experience
C: Framework familiarity
D: Publication count
manager.explanation: Production experience and restraint are the differentiators. Frameworks are learnable; judgement is not quickly acquired.

manager.q: How should you structure an ML project with high uncertainty about feasibility?
opts: A: Time-boxed feasibility spike with defined success criteria and a go/no-go decision before committing to delivery
B: Commit to a full delivery timeline upfront
C: Skip planning entirely
D: Extend the timeline to absorb risk
manager.explanation: Separating feasibility from delivery makes stopping a legitimate outcome rather than a failure.

manager.q: Your ML team consistently misses sprint commitments on model improvement work. What should change?
opts: A: Remove estimation entirely
B: Extend sprints to six weeks
C: Distinguish deterministic engineering work, which can be committed, from research work, which should be time-boxed with review gates
D: Increase accountability pressure
manager.explanation: The problem is applying a delivery framework to research. Separating the two work types fixes the measurement.

manager.q: Why does ML technical debt accumulate faster than conventional software debt?
opts: A: Data dependencies, pipeline coupling, and configuration sprawl create hidden entanglement that ordinary code review does not surface
B: ML teams are less disciplined
C: Frameworks change too often
D: ML code is harder to write
manager.explanation: Changing one feature can silently alter every downstream model. This coupling has no direct analogue in conventional software.

manager.q: How should you fund ML technical debt reduction?
opts: A: It should not require funding
B: Only when velocity collapses
C: As a separate project when things break
D: As a standing allocation of team capacity, typically 15 to 25%, reviewed against a maintained debt register
manager.explanation: Debt work loses every prioritisation contest unless capacity is reserved in advance.

manager.q: Your AI team delivers technically strong work the business does not use. What organisational change helps most?
opts: A: More frequent demos
B: More detailed documentation
C: Embedding a product owner from the business with authority over scope and success criteria
D: Reassigning the team
manager.explanation: Demos communicate but do not change what gets built. Business authority over scope does.

manager.q: Your best ML engineer is at flight risk. What retention lever is most effective in this field?
opts: A: A management promotion
B: A longer notice period
C: Salary increase alone
D: Access to interesting problems, modern tooling, visible impact, and technical growth, alongside competitive pay
manager.explanation: Compensation is necessary but rarely sufficient. Promoting strong engineers into management they do not want is a common retention error.

manager.q: How should you handle an AI project that has failed?
opts: A: Assign accountability to the lead
B: Quietly reassign the team
C: A documented post-mortem focused on decisions and signals rather than individuals, with lessons fed into the intake process
D: Avoid discussing it
manager.explanation: Blameless review preserves the willingness to attempt uncertain work, which is required in this domain.

manager.q: Design a team structure to support 12 production models across 4 business units. What is workable?
opts: A: One engineer per model
B: A platform team owning shared infrastructure and standards, with embedded model owners in each business unit
C: Full outsourcing
D: One large central team owning all 12
manager.explanation: The platform absorbs undifferentiated operational work; embedded owners retain domain accountability. This scales better than either extreme.

manager.q: Which metric best reflects ML team health?
opts: A: Number of experiments run
B: Lines of code
C: Number of models built
D: Time from problem definition to validated production deployment, plus the proportion of deployed models still delivering value
manager.explanation: Output counts encourage volume. Cycle time and sustained value measure whether the team produces useful, durable systems.

manager.q: You must reduce friction between AI delivery and the risk function. What structural change helps most?
opts: A: Involve risk at design stage with pre-agreed criteria by risk tier, replacing late-stage gate reviews
B: Give AI teams an exemption
C: Fewer risk reviews
D: Move risk into the AI team
manager.explanation: Late-stage review is where cost concentrates. Early engagement with known criteria removes rework without weakening control.

manager.q: A team requests a full rewrite of a working but messy ML pipeline. How should you evaluate the request?
opts: A: Approve it; clean code matters
B: Defer indefinitely
C: Decline; it works
D: Require the cost of the current state to be quantified against the rewrite cost and risk, and consider incremental refactoring first
manager.explanation: Rewrites routinely overrun and reintroduce solved bugs. The case must be made in terms of measured cost, not discomfort.

manager.q: Which criterion should carry most weight when evaluating an AI vendor for a regulated use case?
opts: A: Company size
B: Breadth of the feature list
C: Explainability, data governance, evidence of domain-specific validation, and integration feasibility
D: Price and marketing quality
manager.explanation: In regulated contexts, the ability to evidence how the system behaves and where its data came from determines whether you can deploy it at all.

manager.q: What should you ask about a vendor's training data?
opts: A: Only its size
B: Provenance, licensing basis, personal data handling, and representativeness for your population
C: The collection date only
D: The storage format
manager.explanation: Provenance drives both legal exposure and performance in your context. Vague answers here are a material finding.

manager.q: How should you design a vendor proof of concept?
opts: A: Let the vendor choose the dataset and scenarios
B: Compare demo quality across vendors
C: Define success criteria, use your own representative data including edge cases, and agree the evaluation method in advance
D: Run it as long as needed
manager.explanation: Vendor-controlled POCs test the vendor's best case. Pre-agreed criteria on your data test whether it works for you.

manager.q: Which contractual term matters most for an AI system making customer-facing decisions?
opts: A: Contract length
B: Payment schedule
C: Volume discount tiers
D: Liability allocation, indemnification for IP and output-related claims, audit rights, and performance service levels
manager.explanation: Standard software terms rarely address model output risk. These provisions need explicit negotiation.

manager.q: What integration factor is most often underestimated in AI procurement?
opts: A: Licence administration
B: The effort to connect the system to internal data sources with correct access controls and data quality
C: Training delivery
D: User interface design
manager.explanation: Integration and data plumbing routinely exceed licence cost. Scoping it during evaluation avoids budget overrun.

manager.q: What IP question must be settled before deploying a generative AI vendor's output commercially?
opts: A: The hosting location
B: The model's parameter count
C: The vendor's patent portfolio
D: Who owns the output, what indemnity covers infringement claims, and whether training data licensing is defensible
manager.explanation: Indemnification scope varies substantially between providers and is one of the more negotiable and consequential terms.

manager.q: A vendor demonstrates 94% accuracy. What must you establish before accepting the figure?
opts: A: How long the model took to train
B: Whether it was independently audited
C: Whether competitors score higher
D: What dataset, population, and metric definition produced it, and whether it reflects your operating conditions
manager.explanation: Vendor benchmarks come from favourable conditions. A pilot on your own data is the only meaningful test.
